I keep thinking about the way light moves across a wall in the late afternoon. It doesn’t ask for attention. It simply arrives, tilts, and disappears, leaving a warmer patch of paint behind like a secret. Most days I miss it. I’m looking at a screen or rehearsing a conversation or worrying about something that hasn’t happened. But when I do notice, the room changes. It becomes less of a container and more of a companion.

Maybe that’s all attention is: a small rebellion against the blur. We spend so much time rushing toward the next thing that we forget the present is already happening, quietly, without demands. A kettle hums. A dog sighs in sleep. Somewhere a train sounds farther away than it actually is. These details don't improve us or make us productive. They just remind us that we are here, embedded in a world that doesn’t need our commentary.

I used to think writing required big ideas. Now I suspect it only requires honesty about small ones. The way an orange peel curls. The specific ache of an old song. The strange comfort of being unknown in a city. If I can describe those faithfully, maybe I’ve said something true.

So this is me practicing. No thesis, no argument. Just a few minutes of watching the dust float in the afternoon light and trying to say what it felt like. It felt like enough. And maybe that is the whole point—to let the ordinary become visible again, even briefly.
